title: Why Koreans Call Strangers Older Sister

slides.headline: A Korean will call you 'older sister' before they learn your name.
slides.note: It is not a mistake. The language requires it.

slides.headline: The words come from family
slides.body: Eonni (언니), oppa (오빠), hyeong (형), nuna (누나) all literally mean an older sibling. In practice Koreans use them on classmates, coworkers, shop staff and people they met ten minutes ago.

slides.headline: Korean has no easy 'you'
slides.body: There is a word for you, but using it on someone older lands as blunt or rude. So the language reaches for something else, and what it reaches for is a family term.

slides.headline: Age is grammar here
slides.body: Korean verbs change depending on whether you are speaking up or down the age line. You cannot finish a sentence politely until you know who is older. That is why the birth year comes up so fast.

slides.headline: The term does real work
slides.body: Calling someone eonni pulls a stranger into a defined relationship. It sets the speech level, the expectations, and who picks up the bill, in one word.

slides.headline: It goes further than siblings
slides.body: Restaurant staff get called imo (이모), aunt. Older men at a market become samchon (삼촌), uncle. It reads as warmth, not as a demotion.

slides.headline: Here is the reframe
slides.body: In English, 'sir' and 'ma'am' create polite distance. In Korean, 'eonni' does the opposite. It closes distance while staying respectful, which English has almost no word for.

slides.headline: the birth year is often the first question
slides.body: Not small talk. It is the setting that decides which form of every verb both people will use for the rest of the conversation.

slides.headline: So what is going on
slides.body: Korean has no comfortable neutral 'you', so it borrows the family instead. Being called sister is the language solving a problem, not a stranger overstepping.

caption:
If a Korean calls you eonni (언니) or hyeong (형) before learning your name, nothing has gone wrong. The language needs it.

Korean verbs change based on who is older, so a conversation cannot stay polite until that is settled. Kinship terms fix the relationship in one word — and unlike 'sir' or 'ma'am' in English, they close distance instead of creating it.

fact_check: Speech-level rules are simplified here for a 10-slide format; Korean honorifics also depend on social role and setting, not age alone.
Usage of oppa and eonni varies by region, generation and context. Younger speakers use them more loosely than the slides imply.
Imo and samchon for service staff is common but not universal, and some people find it dated.
